source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτά φησιν· εἰ μὲν ἐβούλετο λανθάνειν, τί ἠκούετο ἡ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνὴ κηρύττουσα αὐτὸν υἱὸν θεοῦ; εἰ δ᾿ οὐκ ἐβούλετο λανθάνειν, τί ἐκολάζετο ἢ τί ἀπέθνῃσκε; καὶ οἴεται ἐν τούτοις διαφωνίαν ἐλέγχειν τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ γεγραμμένων, οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι οὔτε πάντα τὰ περὶ αὐτὸν ἐβούλετο πᾶσι καὶ οἷς ἔτυχε γινώσκεσθαι οὔτε πάντα λανθάνειν τὰ καθ᾿ ἑαυτόν. ἡ γοῦν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνὴ κηρύττουσα αὐτὸν εἶναι υἱὸν θεοῦ καὶ λέγουσα· „οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, ἐν ᾧ ηὐδόκησα,“ οὐκ ἀναγέγραπται εἰς ἐπήκοον τοῖς ὄχλοις γεγονέναι, ὅπερ ᾠήθη ὁ Κέλσου Ἰουδαῖος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ ἐν τῷ ὑψηλοτάτῳ ὄρει ἀπὸ τῆς νεφέλης φωνὴ μόνοις ἠκούετο τοῖς συναναβᾶσιν αὐτῷ. καὶ γὰρ τοιαύτη ἐστὶν ἡ θεία φωνὴ, ἀκουομένη μόνοις ἐκείνοις, οὓς βούλεται ἀκούειν ὁ λέγων, οὐδέπω δὲ λέγω ὅτι οὐ πάντως ἐστὶν ἀὴρ πεπληγμένος ἢ πληγὴ ἀέρος ἢ ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγεται ἐν τοῖς περὶ φωνῆς ἡ ἀναγραφομένη φωνὴ τοῦ θεοῦ, διόπερ τῇ κρείττονι τῆς αἰσθητῆς ἀκοῆς καὶ θειοτέρᾳ ἀκούεται. καὶ ἐπὰν βούληται ὁ λέγων μὴ πᾶσιν ἐξάκουστον εἶναι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φωνὴν, ὁ μὲν „ἔχων“ τὰ κρείττονα „ὦτα“ ἀκούει θεοῦ, ὁ δὲ κεκωφωμένος τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀκοὴν ἀναισθητεῖ λέγοντος θεοῦ. ταῦτα μὲν διὰ τὸ τί ἠκούετο ἡ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνὴ ἡ κηρύττουσα αὐτὸν υἱὸν θεοῦ; εἰς δὲ τὸ εἰ οὐκ ἐβούλετο λανθάνειν, τί ἐκολάζετο ἢ τί ἀπέθνῃσκεν; ἀρκεῖ τὰ περὶ τοῦ πάθους ἡμῖν διὰ πλειόνων ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω λελεγμένα.
pass_a_gloss: After these things he says: 'If he wished (βούλομαι) to escape notice (λανθάνω), why was heard (ἀκούω) the voice (φωνή) from heaven proclaiming (κηρύσσω) him son of God? But if he did not wish to escape notice, why was he punished (κολάζω) or why was he dying (ἀποθνῄσκω)?' And he thinks in these things to convict/expose (ἐλέγχω) a disagreement (διαφωνία) of the things written about him, not seeing that neither all the things about him he wished to be known (γινώσκω) to all and to whoever happened (οἷς ἔτυχε), nor all the things concerning himself to escape notice. At any rate the voice from heaven proclaiming him to be son of God and saying: 'This is my son, the beloved (ἀγαπητός), in whom I was well pleased (εὐδοκέω),' is not recorded (ἀναγράφω) to have happened into the hearing (εἰς ἐπήκοον) of the crowds (ὄχλος), which the Jew of Celsus supposed (οἴομαι); but also the voice on the highest (ὑψηλότατος) mountain from the cloud (νεφέλη) was heard only by those having gone up with (συναναβαίνω) him. For such is the divine voice (θεία φωνή), heard only by those whom the speaker wishes to hear; and I do not yet say that the recorded voice of God is not at all (οὐ πάντως) struck air (ἀὴρ πεπληγμένος) or stroke of air (πληγὴ ἀέρος) or whatever is said in the [treatises] about voice, wherefore it is heard by the hearing (ἀκοή) better (κρείττων) than the sense-perceptible (αἰσθητή) and more divine. And whenever the speaker wishes his own voice not to be audible (ἐξάκουστος) to all, the one 'having' the better 'ears' (οὖς) hears God, but the one deafened (κωφόω) in the hearing of the soul (ψυχή) is without perception (ἀναισθητέω) of God speaking. These things on account of 'why was heard the voice from heaven proclaiming him son of God?'; but toward 'if he did not wish to escape notice, why was he punished or why was he dying?' the things about the passion (πάθος) said by us at length (διὰ πλειόνων) in the things above suffice (ἀρκέω).
pass_b_english: After this he says: “If he wished to escape notice, why was the voice from heaven heard proclaiming him Son of God? But if he did not wish to escape notice, why was he punished, or why did he die?” By this he thinks he is exposing a disagreement in what is written about him. He does not see that Jesus wished neither that everything about him should be known to all, to anyone at all, nor that everything concerning himself should remain hidden.

At any rate, the voice from heaven that proclaimed him to be the Son of God and said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), is not recorded to have been within the hearing of the crowds, as Celsus’s Jew supposed. Moreover, the voice from the cloud on the very high mountain was heard only by those who had gone up with him (Matthew 17:1–5; compare Mark 9:2–7; Luke 9:28–35). For the divine voice is of such a kind that it is heard only by those whom the speaker wishes to hear it. I do not yet add that the voice of God recorded in Scripture is by no means struck air, or a stroke of air, or whatever else it is called in the treatises on voice, and that for this reason it is heard by a hearing higher and more divine than the hearing of the senses. And whenever the speaker wishes his voice not to be audible to all, the one who “has” the higher “ears” (Matthew 13:9) hears God, while the one whose soul’s hearing has been deafened does not perceive God speaking.

So much in answer to “Why was the voice from heaven heard proclaiming him Son of God?” As for “If he did not wish to escape notice, why was he punished, or why did he die?”, what we have said at length above about his passion is enough.

choices.why: 'to all and to anyone at all' made 'to all, to anyone at all' (πᾶσι καὶ οἷς ἔτυχε)
Note added that οὐ πάντως could also mean 'not necessarily'

translator_notes: Celsus’s two-part dilemma is in double quotation marks, and Origen repeats both halves at the end. ‘Son of God’ is capitalised because it reports the Christian claim about Christ. Matthew 3:17 is quoted exactly (ηὐδόκησα); Mark 1:11 and Luke 3:22 have ‘you are’. ‘The very high mountain’ renders Origen’s superlative ὑψηλοτάτῳ (Matthew 17:1 and Mark 9:2 have ὄρος ὑψηλόν); the voice from the cloud is Matthew 17:5. ‘Struck air’ (ἀὴρ πεπληγμένος) and ‘stroke of air’ (πληγὴ ἀέρος) are standard philosophical definitions of voice (Stoic and earlier); no source added inline. οὐδέπω δὲ λέγω ὅτι οὐ πάντως is taken as ‘I do not yet add that... is by no means’, a statement Origen holds back for now; οὐ πάντως could also be read ‘not necessarily’. The clause beginning διόπερ is taken as part of what is held back. ‘Has ears’ alludes to the Gospel saying ‘he who has ears, let him hear’ (Matthew 13:9; also Matthew 11:15; Mark 4:9); cited at Matthew 13:9. ‘At length above’ refers to Origen’s earlier discussion of the passion in Book 2.
